text: Τόπον κατάσκιον. Tritissimæ voces κατάσκιος et κατασκιάζειν. Quarum ultimam reduci velim in locum suum, apud Palladium, Dialogo de vita S. Chrysostomi, cap. 18, p. 178 : Εἰς ὕπνον κατέπεσεν, οὔτε τοίχου ἢ πέτρας σκιὰν εὑρίσκων, ἀλλ᾽ ὑπὸ φυτὸν ἀρκεύθινον, ὃ καὶ αὐτὸ ἀμυδρῶς κατασκιάζει. Minime vero κατασκευάζει. Elias in somnum decidit, neque parietis aut saxi inveniens umbram, sed sub juniperi virgulto, quod et ipsum exiliter obumbrat. Nec minus in voce haud absimili erratum t. II Auct. Combef. c. 237 D. In Andreæ Cretensis lambis, φωτὸς καταστράπτοντος αὐτοὺς ἀσκίου. Quos fulguris, lux, in modum blande subit. Cum edendum fuisset ἀσκίου. Φῶς ἄσκιον lumen significat divinum quod umbra caret. Lumine umbræ experte collustrante ipsos.
anchorLine: κατάσκιον (d), προσδοχῶντες τὸν ἐκ τῆς δίψης θάνα-
en: 'A shady place.' The words κατάσκιος and κατασκιάζειν are very common. I should like the latter restored to its place in Palladius, Dialogue on the Life of St John Chrysostom, ch. 18, p. 178: 'He fell asleep, finding no shade of wall or rock, but under a juniper bush, which itself shades only faintly.' Certainly not κατασκευάζει. Elias fell asleep, finding no shade of wall or rock, but under a juniper shrub, which itself shades but thinly. There is no less an error in a similar word in Combefis, Auctarium, vol. 2, col. 237 D: in the iambs of Andrew of Crete, 'φωτὸς καταστράπτοντος αὐτοὺς ἀσκίου' (of a shadowless light flashing upon them): 'whom the light of lightning gently comes upon', when ἀσκίου should have been printed. 'Φῶς ἄσκιον' signifies the divine light that lacks shadow: 'with a light free of shadow shining upon them.'

text: Καυκίῳ. Καυκίον et καυκάλιον infra, cap. 15, ut καῦκος et καῦκα, idem sonant ac Latine caucus, caucum, cauculus, caucellus ; id est calix, scyphus, poculum, patera et vas cavum. Circa quæ omissis aliorum animadversionibus, unum expendam locum, ex Indice ad Nicetæ Annales petitum, Καύκαλον, μίμημα, p. 95 C, ubi narratur de Aarone mago et dicitur : Καὶ προῦχειτο χελώνης ἐκφορον μίμημα, ἔνδον στέγον τῆς χέλυος ἀνθρωπόμορφον εἴκασμα, πεπεδημένον ἄμφω τὼ πόδε, καὶ τὸ στέρνον ἐληλαμένον ἥλῳ διαμπερές. Interpr. : Et simulacrum testudinis prolatum, in quo erat imago hominis, qui ambos pedes habebat in compedibus et pectus clavo transfixum. Verum καύκαλον, vel ut forte scribendum est καυκάλινον, et μίμημα nullatenus quadrant, sed μίμημα respondet voci sequenti εἴκασμα nisi si pro καύκαλον vitiose legerit εἴκελον. Nicetas itaque, mea quidem sententia, explicari debet de cauco et vase concavo ; illiusque verba hoc pacto in Latinum sermonem sunt transferenda : Et depromptum prostabat testudineum vasculum, intra testudinem tegens humanæ formæ imaginem, utroque pede compeditam, et per totum pectus clavo confixam. Nec me præteriit, Salmasium hominem longe doctissimum aliter sentire in Notis ad Spartianum, atque χελώνης καύκαλον exponere testudinis superficiem, quod mihi ideo non placet, tum quia non solum proferebatur superficies testudinis, sed testudo ipsa seu vas e testudine, tum quia coactius videtur interpretamentum. Cogitet etiam prudens lector, utrum in eodem Nicetæ Indice καῦκα, quæ καῦκα est ac ἑταιρίς, erratum sit descriptoris : non enim ausim affirmare, ut et dubito de his in Vita Eudociæ martyris n. 2, Martii 1 : Γέγονε καυκίον ἀμόλυντος, quia vestigia ms. lectionis magis premeret καὶ ὀχεῖον.
anchorLine: τὸ χεῖλος τῆς κολυμβήθρας, καὶ ἐν ξυλίνῳ καυκίῳ (e)
en: 'In a cup.' Καυκίον and καυκάλιον below, ch. 15, like καῦκος and καῦκα, sound the same as Latin caucus, caucum, cauculus, caucellus, that is, a cup, goblet, drinking vessel, dish and hollow vessel. Passing over others' remarks on these, I shall weigh one passage, taken from the Index to the Annals of Nicetas, under Καύκαλον, 'likeness', p. 95 C, where Aaron the magician is described: 'And there was set forth a likeness of a tortoise, within the tortoise-shell a man-shaped image, with both feet fettered and the breast driven through with a nail.' Latin version: 'And a likeness of a tortoise was brought forth, in which was the image of a man who had both feet in fetters and his breast pierced by a nail.' But καύκαλον (or perhaps one should write καυκάλινον) and μίμημα do not fit at all; rather μίμημα corresponds to the following word εἴκασμα, unless the writer misread εἴκελον for καύκαλον. Nicetas therefore, in my opinion, should be explained of a cup and a hollow vessel, and his words rendered into Latin thus: 'And a little tortoise-shell vessel was brought out, covering inside the shell an image of human form, bound by both feet and pierced through the whole breast by a nail.' I am aware that Salmasius, a very learned man, thinks otherwise in his Notes on Spartianus and explains χελώνης καύκαλον as the surface of the tortoise-shell; I dislike this both because not only the surface of the shell was brought forth but the tortoise itself or a vessel of shell, and because the interpretation seems forced. Let the prudent reader also consider whether in the same Index of Nicetas καῦκα, which is the same as ἑταιρίς, is a copyist's error; I dare not affirm it, and I likewise doubt the passage in the Life of Eudocia the martyr, n. 2, March 1: 'Γέγονε καυκίον ἀμόλυντος', since the traces of the manuscript reading would lean more toward 'καὶ ὀχεῖον'.

text: Δρακονάρις seu δρακονάριος. Πατρῶνος δρακιωνάριος. Epist. Theodoriti 59. Et epist. 133 : Θεοδότου τοῦ δρακωναρίου. Leo δρακοναρίους appellat. Latinis draconarii. Lib. xx Ammiani Marcellini : Abstractum sibi torquem, quo ut draconarius utebatur, capiti Juliani imposuit. Reliqua ad draconarios spectantia, δρακοντοφόρους, signiferos, gestatores vexillorum in quibus dracones depicti, e Glossariis criticorumque Commentariis discentar.
anchorLine: ρις (f) τις διηγήσατό μοι λέγων, ὅτι Πόλεμον ἔχομεν
en: 'Draconaris' or 'draconarios'. 'Patronos the draconarios.' Theodoret, Letter 59, and Letter 133: 'of Theodotus the draconarios'. Leo calls them draconarii. In Latin, draconarii. Ammianus Marcellinus, book 20: 'He took off the torque which he used as a draconarius and placed it on Julian's head.' Other matters concerning draconarii (dragon-bearers, standard-bearers, bearers of banners on which dragons are painted) are to be learned from the Glossaries and the critics' Commentaries.

text: Θέκλη. Labitur memoria vir magnus, mihique, dum viveret amicissimus, Henricus Valesius, quando scribit Ad Evagrium, dictam esse Theclam per syncopen pro Theoclea, ut non raro eam appellat Basilius Seleuciensis. Theoclia enim sive Theoclea mater erat, Thecla filia.
anchorLine: σῇ Θέκλῃ (g), καὶ ῥυσάμενος αὐτὴν ἐκ τῶν ἀνόμων
en: 'Thecla.' The memory of a great man, and a most dear friend to me while he lived, Henricus Valesius, slips: when he writes in 'Ad Evagrium' that Thecla is said by syncope for Theoclea, as Basil of Seleucia not rarely calls her. For Theoclia or Theoclea was the mother, Thecla the daughter.

text: Σαρακηνούς. Concilii Lateranensis iv, capitulum 68, est : Περὶ φίγξεως σχήματος Χριστιανῶν, Ἰουδαίων, καὶ Σαρακηνῶν. Ἐν ταῖς (seu potius ἔν τισιν) ἐπαρχίαις παρὰ τῶν Χριστιανῶν τοὺς Ἰουδαίους ἢ Σαρακηνοὺς ἢ τῶν ἐνδυμάτων διαστέλλει διαφορά· ἀλλὰ καὶ ἔν τισιν οὕτως τις ἐπηύξησεν σύγχυσις, ὡς μηδεμίαν διαφορὰν διαιρήσεται, etc. Et primo quidem ad marginem sollicitatur φίγξεως, ut mutetur in σφίγξεως, vel στίξεως. Cum possit esse fixio, a figendo. Deinde vero postrema incommode edundur, facile ex Latinis corrigenda, sic, ὡς μηδεμιᾷ διαφορᾷ διαιρήσεσθαι. De fixione habitus Christianorum, Judæorum, et Saracenorum. In nonnullis provinciis a Christianis Judæos seu Saracenos habitus distinguit diversitas : sed in quibusdam sic quædam inolevit confusio, ut nulla differentia discernantur.
anchorLine: τῆσαι αὐτῷ Σαρακηνοὺς (h) διερχομένους τοὺς τόπους
en: 'Saracens.' Chapter 68 of the Fourth Lateran Council is: 'On the fixing of the dress of Christians, Jews and Saracens. In the provinces [or rather, in some] a difference of dress distinguishes Jews or Saracens from Christians; but in some a confusion has so grown up that they are distinguished by no difference', etc. And first, φίγξεως is queried in the margin, to be changed to σφίγξεως or στίξεως, since it could be 'fixio', from 'fixing'. Then the last part is awkwardly printed and is easily corrected from the Latin, thus: ὡς μηδεμιᾷ διαφορᾷ διαιρήσεσθαι. 'On the fixing of the dress of Christians, Jews and Saracens: in some provinces a difference of dress distinguishes Jews or Saracens from Christians; but in some a confusion has so grown up that they are not distinguished by any difference.'
unreadable: The verb in the Greek of the Council text (ἐπηύξησεν) is small and uncertain in the plate; transcribed as it best reads.

We owe very much to the most distinguished man and our close friend Emericus Bigotius, if only because he brought to light the ancient translation of Nilus's little work On the Eight Vices, by whose help we have uncovered a most elegant reading. text: Ἐκ τῆς χώρας τοῦ Δαρᾶς. Ut in Photio, Theophane, Nilo Doxapatrio Δαρὰς Cedreno et Photio Δαρβᾶς ; apud eumdem Photium minus bene. Pluribus Δάρας. Δάραι Procopio. Stephanus, Δαραί, ὂν ρας (f. ὃ καὶ Δάρας φασὶ, φρούριον Ἀναστασίου πόλεως ; (An Ἀναστασιούπολις, ex Procopio, Theophane et Cedreno) λεγόμενον ὀχυρώτατον. Juxta etymologiam quam tradit Evagrius, lib. iii, cap. 37 ; et post eum Nicephorus, lib. xvi, cap. 37 ; et Auctor Etymologici magni, a Dario illic devicto Interpres nostri Joannis Moschi, ex regione Dora. Hoc est, opinor, Δωρᾶς, vel Δόρας, quemadmodum in ms. Photii apud Holstenium, et Chronici Alexandrini, p. 762 ; quo tamen ultimo in loco suspicari quis posset legendum Δάρας, ob Etymon ὅτι Δαρεῖον Ἀλέξανδρος ἐκεῖ δόρατι ἔκρουσεν. Videndus ad Procopium Alemannus.
anchorLine: ἐκ τῆς χώρας τοῦ Δαρᾶς (k), ὀνόματι
en: 'From the region of Daras.' As in Photius, Theophanes, Nilus Doxapatrius, 'Daras'; Cedrenus and Photius, 'Darbas'; in the same Photius, less well, the plural 'Daras'. 'Darai' in Procopius. Stephanus: 'Darai' [...] (perhaps what they also call Daras, a fortress of the city of Anastasius, [or Anastasiopolis, from Procopius, Theophanes and Cedrenus], said to be very strongly fortified). According to the etymology given by Evagrius, bk 3, ch. 37, and after him Nicephorus, bk 16, ch. 37, and the author of the Etymologicum Magnum, because Darius was defeated there, the translator of our John Moschus has 'from the region Dora'. That is, I think, 'Doras', or 'Doras', as in the manuscript of Photius in Holstenius and the Chronicon Alexandrinum, p. 762; in this last place one might suspect that 'Daras' should be read, on account of the etymon that Alexander struck Darius there with a spear. See Alemannus on Procopius.

text: Ἔβαλεν μετάνοιαν. Ad ea quæ t. II, hæc adjungo novæ lectionis. In Typico S. Sabæ f. 13, seu apud Gretserum, De cruce, c. 1171, C ψάλλοντες καὶ μετανοίας τρεῖς. Emenda et lege βάλλοντες, etiam ex Typici, f. 57, et ex Gretserianis c. 1521 C, 2389 A, 2413 C. Præterea male Combefisius t. I, Maximi p. 644, 722, μετανοῶν mutavit in εὐνοῶν.
anchorLine: μετάνοιαν (n), δοξάζων τὸν Θεόν
en: 'He made a prostration.' To what I said in vol. 2 I add these new readings. In the Typikon of St Sabas, f. 13, or in Gretser, De cruce, col. 1171: 'singing and three prostrations'. Emend and read 'casting', also from the Typikon, f. 57, and from Gretser cols. 1521 C, 2389 A, 2413 C. Moreover Combefis, vol. 1, Maximus pp. 644, 722, wrongly changed 'repenting' (μετανοῶν) into 'well-disposed' (εὐνοῶν).

text: Σευήρου. De quo vide etiam quæ refert Theodorus Rhaithuensis in fine Opusculi de Incarnatione, quæ perperam subjuncta fuere Catechetico Gregorii Nysseni. A Victore Tononensi non semel vocatur princeps hæresis; sed semel hæres ediderunt. Jam vero inter varia quæ scripsit Severus, librum quoque composuit adversus Joannem Cæsariensem Grammaticum concilii Chalcedonensis defensorem, teste Anastasio, Hodegi cap. 6. Ex quo corrigi debet Indiculus a Philippo Labbeo viro bene docto editus in Conspectu novæ editionis Damasceni, p. 54, ubi legitur : Σεβήρου τοῦ δυσσεβοῦς ἐν τῷ κατὰ τοῦ Καχαρέως γραμματικοῦ βιβλίῳ, pro Καισαρέως. A Severo dicti Severitæ et Severiani; quod secundum nomen reddi velim Isaaco Catholico, Invectiva 2, in Armenios, t. II, Auctarii Combefisiani, c. 405 D. Ἡ τοιαύτη αἵρεσις δικαιοῖ τὴν αἵρεσιν Εὐτυχοῦς καὶ Σευηριανοὺς (non autem Σευηριανοῦ) τοὺς λέγοντας, etc. Neque præteribo jocularem ad Cedrenum παρερμηνείαν. Cum enim notasset, falso tamen Cedrenus, aut aliquis ejus Scholiastes, differentiam accentus in nomine Græco Severi, ut Σεῦηρος sit Severus imperator, Σεβῆρος Severus Hæreticus; visum est Xylandro verba Cedrenica : Σεῦηρος ἐβασίλευσεν ἔτη ιζ', μῆνας η'. Σεβῆρος δὲ ὁ αἱρετικὸς λέγεται. Sic vertere, Severus imperavit annos xvii, menses viii. Severus Latinis est, qui Græcis hæreticus, et ad ea annotare, Severus qui sit idem quod Hæreticus, ignoro. Goar autem de truce, rigido, exitiali, quique ideo dici possit αἱρετικός, aut forte ἀναιρετικός, eadem interpretatus est.
anchorLine: ρου (o) ὑπῆρχεν αἱρέσεως. Καὶ διαφόρως ὁ αἱρετι-
en: 'Of Severus.' On him see also what Theodore of Rhaithu reports at the end of his Opusculum on the Incarnation, which was wrongly appended to the Catechetical Oration of Gregory of Nyssa. Victor of Tunnuna more than once calls him 'prince of heresy'; but [the heretics] once published [...]. Among the various things Severus wrote, he also composed a book against John of Caesarea the Grammarian, defender of the Council of Chalcedon, according to Anastasius, Hodegos ch. 6. From this the Index published by the learned Philippe Labbe in the Conspectus of the new edition of Damascene, p. 54, must be corrected, where one reads 'of the impious Severus in the book against the grammarian of Cacares', for 'Caesarea'. Those named after Severus are called Severites and Severians; I would have the second name restored to Isaac Catholicus, Invective 2, Against the Armenians, Combefis Auctarium vol. 2, col. 405 D: 'Such a heresy justifies the heresy of Eutyches, and the Severians (not Severianus) who say', etc. Nor shall I pass over a comical mistranslation in Cedrenus. Cedrenus (or some scholiast of his) having noted, wrongly, a difference of accent in the Greek name Severus, so that Σεῦηρος is the emperor Severus and Σεβῆρος the heretic Severus, Xylander thought fit to render the words of Cedrenus 'Σεῦηρος reigned 17 years, 8 months; Σεβῆρος is called the heretic' as 'Severus reigned 17 years, 8 months. Severus is Latin, which in Greek is heretic', and to annotate that he did not know whether Severus is the same as Heretic. Goar, however, interpreted it of something harsh, rigid, deadly, which could therefore be called αἱρετικός or perhaps ἀναιρετικός.

text: Αἰθίοπα. Huc aliquo modo pertinet locus Palladii Lausiacæ Historiæ cap. 22, extremo, corruptus et ab interprete ex parte præteritus. Αὕτη ἡ ἔνθεος τῆς ἀσκήσεως πολιτεία τοῦ ἀκαταγωνίστου ἀθλητοῦ Μωϋσέως τοῦ τῷ γένει Αἰθίοπος, τὴν δὲ ψυχὴν ἐθίσαντος θείᾳ χάριτι. Quæ sunt interpreti tantum : Hæc est religiosa et sancta vita quam egit invictus athleta Moses Æthiops. Tu vero sic mecum sic lege, αἰθήσαντος, ac verte : Hæc est divina religiosaque vita invicti athletæ Mosis, qui genere fuit Æthiops, animam autem suam divina gratia inflammavit. Αἰθίοψ et αἰθήσαντος eleganter et apte sibi mutuo respondet.
anchorLine: θεωρῶ ἄνδρα⁶¹ Αἰθίοπα (p), ῥάκη περιβε-
en: 'Ethiopian.' To this has some relevance a passage at the end of ch. 22 of Palladius's Lausiac History, corrupted and in part passed over by the translator. The Greek reads: 'This is the God-inspired way of ascetic life of the unconquered athlete Moses, Ethiopian by race, whose soul was trained by divine grace.' The translator has only: 'This is the religious and holy life which the invincible athlete Moses the Ethiopian led.' But read with me 'αἰθήσαντος' (having kindled) and render: 'This is the divine and religious life of the invincible athlete Moses, who was an Ethiopian by race, but kindled his soul with divine grace.' 'Aithiops' and 'aithesantos' answer to one another elegantly and aptly.

Unde apud Lambecium, De bibliotheca Cæsarea, lib. iv, cod. 164, n. 7, quæstio de nomine ejus qui Christum percussit. Et lib. v, cod. 289, p. 243, inter Georgii Calybæ ἐρωταποκρίσεις, tricesima secunda est, περὶ τοῦ ῥαπίσαντος τὸν Χριστόν : Servum illum Caiphæ, qui in Domini Christi faciem colaphum impegerat. anchorLine: Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ῥαπίσας (q) ἐπὶ τῆς σιαγόνος
en: 'The one who struck', etc. Malchus, in Chrysostom, hom. 82 on John; in Theophanes Cerameus, hom. 27; Euthymius; others. Whence in Lambecius, On the Caesarean Library, bk 4, cod. 164, n. 7, the question of the name of him who struck Christ. And bk 5, cod. 289, p. 243, among the Questions and Answers of George Calybes, the thirty-second is 'On the one who struck Christ': that servant of Caiaphas who dealt a blow to the face of the Lord Christ. In Damascene, oration 2 on the Assumption of the Mother of God. Everyone knows the opinion of Cyril of Alexandria.

text: Λεκτικίῳ. t. I, p. 413 B, epis. t. 14 S. Chrysostomi, in Vita Maximi confessoris, n. 39 ; Vita et Martyrio S. Eudociæ, n. 39, et apud alios a Meursio citatos. Hinc λεκτικάριος, etiam in epistola Theodoriti 110 ; Anonymus in Vita Chrysostomi, Savilianæ editionis, t. VIII, p. 358 ; l. ix et xvi, λεκτίκιον habet, forsan non absque menda. Porro locus e Vita Maximi dignus est qui hic ascribatur, Ἐπεὶ δὲ, ὡς ὁ λόγος ἔφη, πρὸς τὴν ὑπερορίαν τὸν θεῖον ἀπήνεγκαν Μάξιμον, πολλὰ μὲν συνέβη τοῦτον παθεῖν κατὰ τὴν ὁδόν, καὶ πολλὰς ὑπομεῖναι τὰς ἀλγηδόνας, οἷα μήτ᾽ εἰς λεκτίκιον καθεσθῆναι δυνάμενον, τῷ πάντῃ κατειργάσθαι τοῖς πόνοις, καὶ ταῖς μυρίαις τετρυχῶσθαι ὀδύναις. Ἀμέλει καὶ εἴς τι χαλάδριον βέργεσι πεπλεγμένον τοῦτον ἐνθέμενοι μόλις καὶ κόπῳ διαβαστάζοντες, τὴν μακρὰν ὁδὸν ἐκείνην ἀπήγαγον. S. Maximum itaque, ut relatum est, in exsilium deportatum, contigit in via multa pati, multasque subire ærumnas, et doloribus conflictari, cum nec jumento nec lectica sedere posset, omnino scilicet confectus laboribus, innumerisque angoribus attritus. Quamobrem gestatorio vimineo grabbato imponunt, et vix ægreque gestantes, longo illo itinere abducunt. Quia per illum emendatio et lux oboritur vocabulo corrupto et obscuro, quod legitur in Vita Dosithei apud Dorotheum Corderii : Ἔστρωννυε δὲ τοῖς ἀρρώστοις πάνυ καλῶς· τοιοῦτος δὲ ἦν περὶ τὸν λογισμὸν ἐλεύθερος καὶ ἐξαγγελτικός, ὅτι πολλάκις ἐν ὅσῳ ἐφιλοκάλει στρῶσαι, εἶδε τὸν μακάριον παρερχόμενον, καὶ λέγει αὐτῷ· Κύριε, κύριε, λέγει μοι ὁ λογισμός, Καλῶς στρωννύεις. Καὶ ἀπεκρίνατο ἐκεῖνος, Βαβαί, κύριε, ἰδοὺ εἶ καλὸς βρεγγάριος vel βεργγάριος : μὴ γὰρ καλὸς μοναχός. Apparet enim ex βέργεσι scribi debere βεργάριος, Virgarius, hoc est stratorum vimineorum adornator. Cæterum ægrotis lectulos commodissime sternebat : adeo autem ingenuus et liber erat in cogitationibus suis manifestandis, ut non raro cum lectulos egregie stravisset, ac beatum Dorotheum illuc transire videret, ei diceret : Domine, domine, cogitatio mihi dicit, eleganter lectulos sternis ; et respondit ei ille : Papæ domine, ecce bonus es virgarius, lectorum seu ex virgis stratorum constructor, non vero bonus monachus
anchorLine: χίῳ (t) ἐπωχεῖτο, τῷ δὲ κληρικῷ ἐπὶ ἀλόγῳ καθ-
en: 'In a litter.' Vol. 1, p. 413 B; letters, vol. 14 of St Chrysostom; in the Life of Maximus the Confessor, n. 39; Life and Martyrdom of St Eudocia, n. 39, and in others cited by Meursius. Hence 'lektikarios', also in Theodoret's letter 110; the Anonymous in the Life of Chrysostom, Savile's edition, vol. 8, p. 358; at ix and xvi it has 'lektikion', perhaps not without error. Moreover a passage from the Life of Maximus deserves to be set down here: 'When, as the account said, they carried the divine Maximus off into exile, many things happened to him on the road, and he endured many pains, being unable to sit even in a litter, since he was entirely worn out with labours and wasted with countless pangs. Indeed they put him in a basket of woven withies and with difficulty and toil carried him along that long road.' So St Maximus, deported into exile, as related, happened to suffer much on the way, and endure many hardships and be afflicted with pains, since he could sit neither on a beast nor in a litter, being entirely worn out with labours and ground down by countless anguish. For this reason they put him on a wicker couch and, bearing him with difficulty and distress, carried him away on that long journey. Because by it emendation and light dawn upon a corrupt and obscure word read in the Life of Dositheus in Dorotheus (Cordier): 'He spread beds for the sick very well; and he was so free and forthcoming about his thoughts that often, while he was glad to be spreading, he saw the blessed one passing by and said to him: Lord, lord, my thought tells me, You make the beds well. And he answered, Bravo, lord, behold you are a good bregarios or bergarios; for [you are] not a good monk.' It appears that from 'bergesi' one should write 'bergarios', Virgarius, that is, a maker of wicker beds. Moreover he made beds for the sick most comfortably; and he was so frank and free in disclosing his thoughts that often when he had made the beds very well and saw the blessed Dorotheus pass by he would say to him: Lord, lord, my thought tells me you make the beds elegantly; and the other replied: Well, lord, you are a good virgarius, a builder of beds or of wickerwork, but not a good monk'

text: Ἠλίαν. Φλαβιανόν. Non facile concesserim Theodoreto lectori ac Theophani chronographo, Heliam Hierosolymorum et Flavianum Antiochenum anathema dixisse concilio Chalcedonensi. Colligo magis ex Evagrio et Nicephoro, atque ex Cyrillo Scythopolitano in Vita S. Sabæ, loco citato, act. 1 et 5 synodi vii, beatos antistites multa quidem variaque œconomia, necnon erga Anastasium imperatorem adulatione usos fuisse, numquam tamen aperte voluisse synodum anathematizare. Quo de ultimo Soterichus et Xenaias hæretici querelas ad imperatorem detulerunt, referente ipso Theophane.
anchorLine: Ἠλίαν μὲν εἰς Αἰλὰν, Φλαβιανὸν (u) δὲ εἰς Πέτραν.
en: 'Elias. Flavian.' I should not readily grant that Theodore the Lector and Theophanes the chronographer are right in saying that Elias of Jerusalem and Flavian of Antioch anathematized the Council of Chalcedon. I gather rather from Evagrius and Nicephorus, and from Cyril of Scythopolis in the Life of St Sabas, in the place cited, and from acts 1 and 5 of the seventh synod, that the blessed prelates used much and various accommodation, and flattery toward the emperor Anastasius, but never openly wished to anathematize the synod. About this last point the heretics Soterichus and Xenaias brought complaints to the emperor, as Theophanes himself reports.

text: Ἐκκλησίας, καὶ Φωτίου ἁγιωτάτου πατριάρχου, ἀκοινωνησίας ἐπιτιμίῳ τοῦ σώματος καὶ αἵματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ, καὶ τῆς τῶν πιστῶν συνάξεως τε καὶ συναυλίας καθυποβάλλει, ἕως ἂν ἐπιμένωσι τῇ ἀποστασίᾳ. Id est : Sancta synodus eos qui a sancta Dei Ecclesia, sanctissimoque patriarcha Photio abscesserunt, censuræ excommunicationis a perceptione corporis et sanguinis Christi, et a conventu contubernioque cum fidelibus, subjicit, quandiu in apostasia et defectione permanserint. Ineptè editum fuit ἀπατήσαντας, et versum eos qui decipiunt.
en: [...] Church, and of the most holy patriarch Photius, subjects them to the penalty of excommunication from the body and blood of Christ and from the assembly and company of the faithful, so long as they persist in apostasy. That is: The holy synod subjects those who have withdrawn from the holy Church of God and from the most holy patriarch Photius to the censure of excommunication from the reception of the body and blood of Christ, and from the assembly and fellowship with the faithful, as long as they remain in apostasy and defection. 'Apatesantas' was foolishly printed, and translated 'those who deceive'.

text: Μακεδόνιον. Exsilium Macedonii verbis memoralibus et valde observandis refertur a Liberato, Breviarii, cap. 19 : Hoc tempore, inquit, Macedonius Constantinopolitanus episcopus, ab Imperatore Anastasio dicitur expulsus, tamquam Evangelia falsasset, et maxime illud Apostoli dictum : « Quia apparuit in carne, justificatum est in spiritu. » Hunc enim immutasse, ubi habet, ὃς, id est qui, monosyllabum Græcum, littera mutata o in ω vertisse, et fecisse ὡς, id est, ut esset Deus, apparuit per carnem. Tanquam Nestorianus ergo culpatus expellitur per Severum monachum. Et primo quidem ad ea : Quia apparuit in carne, observo, Liberatum, I Tim. iii, 16, aut legisse in Græco ὡς, aut Latinum
anchorLine: Μακεδόνιον (x) τοὺς πατριάρχας Κωνσταντινουπό-
en: 'Macedonius.' The exile of Macedonius is reported in memorable and much-to-be-observed words by Liberatus, Breviary, ch. 19: 'At this time,' he says, 'Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople, is said to have been expelled by the emperor Anastasius, as though he had falsified the Gospels, and especially that saying of the Apostle: "Who was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit."' [It is said] that he changed, where it has 'hos', that is 'who', a Greek monosyllable, by altering the letter o to omega, and made 'hos', that is, 'as God', 'he was manifested through the flesh'. So, accused as a Nestorian, he is expelled through the monk Severus. And first, as to this: 'Who was manifested in the flesh', I observe that Liberatus (cf. 1 Tim. 3:16) either read 'hos' in the Greek, or the Latin [...] (breaks off at the foot of the page).
